unit.title: Properties of Materials
unit.blurb: Physical and chemical properties of materials, how metals and non-metals differ, and why alloys are harder than pure metals.

O1.t: Describe physical properties: strength, hardness, ductility, malleability, melting point, conductivity and density.

O2.t: Describe chemical properties: reactivity, flammability, acidity, corrosiveness and toxicity.

O3.t: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals, including exceptions such as carbon.

O4.t: Explain why alloys have different properties from pure metals and give uses of alloys.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 7: Properties of Materials.
The first aeroplane, built in 1903, was made of wood and fabric.
Today's jets use aluminium and titanium alloys, carbon fibre and plastics: light,
strong and long-lasting. What properties make these materials so useful?
Let's find out!
Look at a diamond.
Is it shiny or dull?
Hard or soft? Warm or cold to the touch?
When you answer, you are describing its properties: the way a material behaves.
Physical properties can be measured or observed without changing the substance,
often using our senses.
They include strength, hardness, melting point, conductivity and density.
Chemical properties can only be observed when the material reacts with another substance,
and it may become something new.
They include reactivity, flammability, acidity and toxicity.
Strength is how well a material withstands forces or supports weight without breaking.
If we knock a glass jug and a metal jug against a hard surface,
the glass cracks, but the metal jug survives.
The metal is stronger.
Hardness means not being easily scratched.
A nail scratches a plastic bowl, but not a metal bowl,
so the metal is harder than the plastic.
The Mohs scale rates hardness from 1, the softest, talc, to 10,
the hardest, diamond. A mineral can scratch anything with a lower number.
Everyday objects fit on the scale too: a fingernail is about 2.5,
glass about 5.5, a steel nail 6.5, and a drill bit 8.5.
A material is ductile if it can be stretched into wires without breaking.
Gold and copper are very ductile.
A material is malleable if it can be hammered or rolled into a new shape.
Aluminium is rolled into foil, and metals are hammered into tools,
horseshoes and jewellery.
A material is flexible if it bends without breaking.
Metal wire is flexible, but a pencil snaps, so it is not.
The melting point is the temperature at which a substance melts,
and the boiling point is the temperature at which it boils.
Different substances have very different values.
Nitrogen boils at minus 196 degrees Celsius,
so at room temperature it is a gas.
Water melts at 0 and boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
Gold melts at 1064 degrees,
and aluminium boils at a scorching 2480 degrees Celsius!
Most metals have high melting points,
which is why they are solid at room temperature.
Liquid nitrogen is so cold that it boils as soon as it is poured,
freezing whatever it touches.
Three spoons, made of steel, wood and plastic, stand in hot water.
A small bead of butter is stuck near the top of each handle.
Predict: which bead will melt and fall first?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The spoons are the same size and stand in the same hot water.
After three minutes, the butter on the steel spoon has melted and fallen off.
The beads on the wooden and plastic spoons have not moved.
Explain what you saw.
Steel is a metal, and metals are good thermal conductors:
heat travels quickly through them, up to the butter.
Wood and plastic are thermal insulators, so heat travels through them very slowly.
That is why saucepans have metal bases but plastic or wooden handles.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
We use many electrical devices every day,
so they must contain materials that conduct electricity.
Copper is used in wires because it is a good conductor,
and it's ductile too.
Electricity can be dangerous, so wires are covered with plastic, an electrical insulator,
which stops electricity passing through and protects us from shocks.
Imagine leaving a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in a pot of boiling pasta.
Which gets hot first?
The metal spoon! Most metals are good thermal conductors.
Wood, plastic and silicone are thermal insulators,
which is why cooking utensils are made from them.
Two blocks, each one cubic centimetre: one silver and one wood.
Which is heavier? The silver block has a mass of 10.5 grams,
but the wood only 0.9 grams.
Density measures how much matter is packed into a space.
Silver has more atoms in each cubic centimetre,
so it is denser than wood.
Very dense materials, like most metals, sink in water, while less dense materials,
like wood, float.
So why don't steel ships sink?
Think about all the air inside the hull,
which makes the ship as a whole less dense than water.
Here are the densities of six materials, in grams per cubic centimetre.
Water has a density of 1 gram per cubic centimetre.
Wood and ice are less dense than water, so they float.
Aluminium, iron and gold are denser, so a solid lump of them sinks.
Gold is almost twenty times denser than water.
Pause and decide: will a solid block of aluminium float or sink in water?

captions: Iron is hard and strong.
But in wet conditions it combines with oxygen to form a flaky,
red-brown substance: iron oxide, or rust.
Rusting is a chemical property of iron,
so pure iron is a poor choice outdoors.
Reactivity describes how easily a material reacts.
Sodium, a soft shiny metal,
is so reactive that it reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen gas.
The opposite of reactive is inert.
Gold is very unreactive: it doesn't react with air, so it stays shiny,
which makes it perfect for jewellery.
Inert gases are also used inside some lamps.
Three iron nails are set up in test tubes.
Tube A has air and water.
Tube B has dry air only, with a drying agent.
Tube C has boiled water covered with oil, so there is no air.
Predict: which nail will rust?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The tubes are left for one week.
Only the nail in tube A has rusted.
The nails in tubes B and C are still shiny.
Explain what you saw.
Rusting is a chemical change: iron reacts with oxygen from the air,
but only when water is also there, to make iron oxide.
Tube B had air but no water.
Tube C had water but no air.
So iron needs both oxygen and water to rust.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Flammability is the ability to burn.
When wood burns, it combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide,
water vapour and other gases.
Fuels like petrol are flammable too.
Many substances are acidic or alkaline.
The pH scale runs from 0, very acidic, through 7, neutral, to 14,
very alkaline. Lemon juice is acidic, while many household cleaners are alkaline.
Corrosive substances destroy materials, including living tissue, on contact.
Batteries left too long in a device can leak corrosive substances.
Toxicity is how poisonous a substance is.
Pesticides kill insects but can harm people and the environment.
Lead, arsenic and mercury are toxic elements that harmed people in the past.

captions: Elements are classified as metals or non-metals.
Most elements are metals, like iron, silver and copper.
There are fewer non-metals, but they combine to form plastics, sugar,
water and petrol.
Metals are usually solid at room temperature with high melting points,
they conduct electricity and heat, and they are shiny.
Non-metals are often gases with low melting points, they are insulators,
and they are dull.
Metals are malleable, ductile, strong and dense.
Non-metals are usually brittle, weak and less dense.
There are exceptions! Diamond is a form of carbon, a non-metal.
But unlike most non-metals, it is shiny,
extremely hard and has a very high melting point.
Graphite, used in pencils, is also carbon.
It has a high melting point and, unusually for a non-metal,
it conducts electricity. But it is soft and brittle.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon.
Their atoms are joined in different ways, so their properties are very different.
Engineers choose each material because of its properties.
Look at these four everyday objects.
A saucepan has a steel base, because metals conduct heat to the food,
and a plastic handle, because plastic is a thermal insulator.
An electric cable has copper inside, which is ductile and conducts electricity,
covered by PVC plastic, an electrical insulator.
A pencil uses graphite, a form of carbon.
Its layers slide off easily, leaving a mark on the paper.
Some drill tips are coated with diamond, the hardest natural material,
so they can cut through rock and glass.
Every use matches a property.

made of plastic or aluminium instead of iron?

captions: In a pure metal,
all the atoms are the same size and are arranged in neat layers.
Push hard enough, and the layers slide over each other.
That's why pure metals are malleable and ductile, but also quite soft.
An alloy is a mixture, so it has atoms of different sizes.
The layers are no longer regular, so they can't slide easily.
That makes alloys harder and stronger than pure metals,
and cracks don't spread through them so easily.
You can model this with towers of same-sized bricks and mixed-sized bricks!
Alloys can be designed with exactly the properties we need.
Bronze, copper mixed with tin, is much stronger than either metal alone.
It was first used about 5300 years ago,
giving its name to the Bronze Age.
Stainless steel contains iron, chromium, nickel and carbon; it is shiny,
strong and doesn't rust, so it's used for sinks and cutlery.
Sterling silver, silver mixed with copper, is harder than soft pure silver.
Titanium alloy is strong, light, resists corrosion and is not toxic,
so it's used in aircraft, racing bikes and hip implants.
In 2023, Australian scientists developed a cheaper titanium alloy using oxygen and iron.
This chart compares the strength of three pure metals with an alloy of each,
measured as the pulling force a material can take before it breaks.
The values are approximate.
Pure aluminium is weak,
but an aluminium alloy used in aircraft is about five times stronger.
Bronze is stronger than pure copper,
and steel is about twice as strong as pure iron.
In every pair, the alloy is stronger.

kids.d: Strength • hardness (Mohs 1–10) • ductile, malleable, flexible • melting point • conductors/insulators • density.
Reactivity (iron rusts, sodium + water, gold inert) • flammability • pH • corrosive • toxic.
Shiny, conductors, malleable vs dull, brittle insulators • exceptions: diamond, graphite.
